tip: To ask for directions, Greek asks about the road: ρώτησα για τον δρόμο (rótisa ya ton dhrómo = I asked about the way).
'There was traffic' uses έχω (ékho = have): είχε κίνηση (íkhe kínisi = there was traffic).
Πουθενά (puthená) flips by context: 'anywhere' in questions – πήγατε πουθενά; (píghate puthená) – but 'nowhere' with δεν (dhen).
Ακριβώς after a time = sharp: στις εννιά ακριβώς (stis enyá akrivós = at nine sharp).
Το αφεντικό (to afendikó = the boss) is neuter, even for a man: μίλησα με το αφεντικό (mílisa me to afendikó).
Adding εσύ stresses WHO: οργάνωσες εσύ; (orghánoses esí = was it YOU who organized it?)
Μου (mu) adds a second accent when the word's own stress sits three syllables from the end: ο συνάδελφός μου (o sinádhelfós mu = my colleague).
You phone TO someone: τηλεφώνησα στην εταιρεία (tilefónisa stin etería = I called the company) – with nouns, τηλεφωνώ (tilefonó) takes σε (se).
The έ- (e-) in έγραψα (éghrapsa = I wrote) only carries stress. When stress moves, it drops: γράψαμε (ghrápsame = we wrote).
No 'a' before jobs: έγινε γιατρός (éyine yatrós = she became a doctor) – after become or be, professions normally drop the article.
Μπόρεσες; (bóreses = did you manage?) – this past of μπορώ (boró) usually means a one-off success, 'managed to', not just general ability.
Background weather takes the ongoing past: έκανε κρύο (ékane krío = it was cold).
Greek opens the door TO someone: άνοιξες την πόρτα στη γάτα; (ánikses tin pórta sti gháta = did you open the door for the cat?) – σε (se), not για (ya).
Κοιμήθηκα (kimíthika = I slept) looks passive but isn't – sleep, remember and fear only have passive-shaped forms, so their past ends in -θηκα (-thika).
Γνώρισα (ghnórisa) = met for the first time. Meeting up with someone you already know is usually είδα (ídha = I saw).
English 'have you met' is plain past in Greek: γνώρισες; (ghnórises) covers both 'did you meet' and 'have you met' – no 'have done' tense needed.
Little words like μου (mu) normally sit right before the verb: μου είπε (mu ípe = he told me).
'To you' normally comes before the verb: σου έδωσα (su édhosa = to-you I-gave) – the little word lands in front.
You laugh WITH something in Greek: γέλασαν με το αστείο (yélasan me to astío = they laughed at the joke).
Turning an age uses γίνομαι (yínome = become) + χρονών: έγινε δέκα χρονών (éyine dhéka khronón = he turned ten).
Πάω βόλτα (páo vólta) = go for a stroll: πήγαμε βόλτα (píghame vólta = we went for a walk).
Ο μικρός / η μικρή (o mikrós / i mikrí) = the kid, an affectionate everyday word: για τον μικρό (ya ton mikró).
The of-form follows the thing owned – reverse of the English 's: το φαγητό της γάτας (to fayitó tis ghátas = the food of-the-cat = the cat's food).
Μαθαίνω (mathéno) is both learn and find out: έμαθες τα νέα; (émathes ta néa = did you hear the news?).
Τη βοήθειά σου (ti voíthiá su = your help) has two accents: with σου (su) attached, stress would sit too far from the end, so a second accent is added.
Βγαίνω για (vyéno ya) = go out for: βγήκαμε για ποτό (vyíkame ya potó = we went out for a drink).
Παίρνω τηλέφωνο (pérno tiléfono) = to phone someone: πήρες τηλέφωνο; (píres tiléfono = did you call?)
One vowel is the whole difference: κάνετε (kánete = you do) vs κάνατε (kánate = you did). Listen for the a.
'Used to' is built into the verb form itself: έμενα (émena = I used to live) – no extra words needed.
Repeated habits take the ongoing past: πηγαίναμε κάθε καλοκαίρι (piyéname káthe kalokéri = every summer we went).
